cards.statement: With `ansible-pull`, each managed node checks out playbooks from Git and runs them on itself.
cards.explanation: Pull mode reverses Ansible's default push model: a crontab on the node runs ansible-pull, which fetches the configuration and manages that machine locally.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Glossary (14) Pull Mode entry confirmed: "ansible-pull works by checking configuration orders out of Git on a crontab and then managing the machine locally", and push mode is the default. Within the prompt's ansible-pull scope (glossary).

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.19, `{{ ['web1', 'web2'] | replace('web', 'db') }}` returns a string instead of a list.
cards.explanation: replace works on strings, so it turns the list into text, and 2.19 removed the final literal-evaluation pass that used to parse such text back into a list. Use map('replace', ...) to keep a list.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. porting_guide_core_2.19.html confirmed: replace "operates only on strings. The filter silently converts the list input to a string", the old literal evaluation hid it, and map('replace', ...) keeps a list. Names the release as the version rule requires.

cards.statement: With DEFAULT_VAULT_ID_MATCH set, Ansible rejects a password that differs from one already used with the same vault ID.
cards.explanation: Ansible does not tie a vault ID label to one password, even with DEFAULT_VAULT_ID_MATCH enabled, so two files can carry the same label with different passwords.
cards.reason: Wording lens fix merged: the binding is now named directly instead of the vague 'new password ... already used elsewhere'. The lens's proposed text was 130 characters, so it was shortened to 118 without changing the fact. Fact lens keeps the fact. vault_managing_passwords.html confirmed: "Even with the DEFAULT_VAULT_ID_MATCH setting enabled, Ansible does not enforce using the same password every time you use a particular vault ID label."

cards.statement: Passing several `--vault-id` options makes one ansible-playbook run read content encrypted with different passwords.
cards.explanation: Give one --vault-id label@source per password, for example dev@dev-password plus prod@prompt, and a single run can decrypt vaulted files and values made with each of them.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. vault_using_encrypted_content.html confirmed: "passing multiple --vault-id options to specify the vault IDs ... and sources for the passwords (prompt, file, script)" with the example `ansible-playbook --vault-id dev@dev-password --vault-id prod@prompt site.yml`. Avoids the try-order claim.

cards.statement: `throttle: 1` on a delegated task that edits one shared file makes Ansible apply the edits one host at a time.
cards.explanation: Delegated tasks still run in parallel forks, so several play hosts can write one delegated file at once and overwrite each other. throttle: 1, serial: 1 or a run_once loop serializes the writes.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. playbooks_delegation.html confirmed: delegation "does not handle concurrency issues (multiple forks writing to the same file)", forks still run in parallel and overwrite each other, and the remedies are run_once with a loop, serial: 1, or throttle: 1 at task level. This is r13 scope.

cards.statement: A delegated host inherits the variables of the play host that delegates the task.
cards.explanation: Delegation copies none of the delegating host's host or group variables onto the delegated-to host, which keeps its own inventory variables.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. playbooks_delegation.html confirmed: "The host to which a task is delegated does not inherit variables from the host that is delegating the task." The explanation now makes no claim about module-argument templating, as the delegation wording rule requires.

cards.statement: With `-i first.yml -i second.yml`, a variable set for one group in both files takes the `first.yml` value.
cards.explanation: When two -i sources set the same group's variable, the source given later on the command line wins, so the value here comes from second.yml.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. intro_inventory.html confirmed: Ansible merges variables in the order the -i parameters are passed, and "-i staging -i production" gives myvar = 2, so the later source wins.

cards.statement: With a role `web` in both `roles/` beside the playbook and `roles_path`, Ansible loads the `roles_path` copy.
cards.explanation: The playbook's adjacent roles/ directory takes priority over roles_path.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. playbooks_reuse_roles.html confirmed the search order: collections, then roles/ relative to the playbook file, then the configured roles_path, then the playbook directory.

cards.statement: After `ansible.builtin.set_fact` sets `release: new`, later tasks read the play `vars` value `release: old`.
cards.explanation: A regular `ansible.builtin.set_fact` host variable outranks play `vars`, so later tasks read `new`.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. playbooks_variables.html precedence list confirmed: Play vars (12) rank below Registered vars and set_facts (19). Cached set_facts sit lower, which the explanation's 'regular' hedges correctly.

cards.statement: When a play and one of its tasks both set `remote_user`, Ansible uses the play's value for that task.
cards.explanation: A task's remote_user overrides the play's value; the more specific keyword wins.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. general_precedence.html confirmed: "Within playbook keywords ... the more specific wins against the more general: play (most general) ... tasks (most specific)".

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.package` converts the name `libyaml-dev` to `libyaml-devel` when it runs on a Red Hat host.
cards.explanation: package delegates to the host's package manager module; the playbook supplies distribution-appropriate names.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. package_module.html confirmed: "This module acts as a proxy to the underlying package manager module" and "this module will not 'translate' them per distribution", with libyaml-dev and libyaml-devel as the page's own example.
